title: Window arithmetic
prompt: With left edge `l` and right edge `r` (both inclusive), the window length is…
explanation: Inclusive-inclusive ranges have length end - start + 1. Off-by-one here is THE most common sliding window bug.

title: Drill: max window sum
prompt: From memory: return the maximum sum of any contiguous window of exactly `k` elements (1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length). Build the first window, then slide with add-enter/subtract-leave.

solution.explanation: Initialize best with the FIRST window (not 0!) so all-negative arrays work.

hints: Neighbouring windows share k-1 elements. How much actually changes when you slide by one?
Sum the first k elements, then slide: one element enters on the right, one leaves on the left.
`windowSum += nums[r] - nums[r - k];` — and start `best` at the first window, not 0.

title: Drill: shortest window with sum >= target
prompt: From memory (variable window): given positive `nums` and a `target`, return the length of the SHORTEST contiguous subarray whose sum is >= target, or 0 if none. Grow right, shrink left while the sum still qualifies.

solution.explanation: Positive values make the window sum monotonic in both edges, so once `[l..r]` qualifies, the only way to find something shorter ending at r is to move l. Both pointers only move forward, so total work is O(n); space O(1).

hints: With only positive numbers, extending a window always increases its sum. What does that tell you about when to shrink?
Grow `r` every step; while the window already reaches the target, it is a candidate — record it and try shrinking from the left.
`while (sum >= target) { best = Math.min(best, r - l + 1); sum -= nums[l++]; }`

title: Template recall: variable window
prompt: From memory: longest substring without repeating characters — grow right, shrink left while invalid.
explanation: The window is invalid while it already holds `c`; removing from the left (and advancing `l` in the same expression) shrinks it until `c` fits. Inclusive window length is `r - l + 1`. `l` only moves forward, so the whole scan is O(n).

title: Why pop from the back?
prompt: Sliding Window Maximum keeps a deque of indices. When `nums[r]` arrives, why is it safe to `pollLast()` every index whose value is smaller than `nums[r]`?
options: Those elements are smaller AND leave the window earlier than r, so they can never be a window maximum again
The deque must stay sorted by index
To keep the deque size at most k
Smaller elements are already out of the window
explanation: An older, smaller element is dominated: every future window containing it also contains `nums[r]`, which is bigger. Dropping dominated elements keeps values decreasing front→back, so the front is always the max. `pollFirst` handles the separate case of the front sliding out of the window.
